hints: Look at point P on the displacement-distance graph at $t=0$: it is at zero displacement on a slope that rises to the right.
For a wave travelling to the right, the string to the left arrives later at P - use the slope to decide if P must move up or down next.
Recall a particle on the string performs SHM about zero, so its velocity-time graph is sinusoidal with maximum speed at zero displacement.
walkthrough: Identify the state of P at $t=0$: displacement $y=0$ and the displacement-distance slope $dy/dx$ is positive because the curve passes upward through P.
State the rule for a transverse progressive wave moving in the $+x$ direction: a positive spatial slope means the particle velocity is downward. In symbols, $v = -c(dy/dx)$ where $c$ is wave speed.
Therefore at $t=0$, P has zero displacement but negative maximum velocity because equilibrium is where SHM speed is greatest.
After $t=0$, P will execute SHM, so its velocity must vary sinusoidally with time with period equal to the wave period, starting from $-v_{max}$.
Graph C starts at $0$ and goes positive, and graph B is triangular starting at $0$, so neither matches a negative-maximum sinusoidal start. This is option D.

options.A: Particle P oscillates in SHM, so its velocity cannot stay constant at a positive value.
options.B: The velocity of SHM is sinusoidal, not triangular, and it does not start at zero moving upward for this wave.
options.C: This sine curve starts at zero and goes positive, which would mean P starts moving up, opposite to the motion caused by the rightward wave.
options.D: P is at equilibrium at $t=0$ moving downward at maximum speed, so velocity starts at a negative maximum and varies sinusoidally.
